strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practically appealing: leverage the geometric structure already encoded in a pretrained goal-conditioned value function to build a graph over dataset states and perform shortest-path search at test time, without any retraining, additional supervision, or online interaction.

Strong empirical improvements are demonstrated across three distinct base learners (HIQL, GCIQL, QRL) on OGBench's hardest giant-maze stitching tasks, with some settings going from near-0% success to 80-98% success, which is a substantial and convincing effect.

The method is shown to generalize beyond value-derived distances to a simple domain-specific (body-position) metric, supporting the claim that the framework is agnostic to the source of the distance signal.

Thorough ablations isolate the contributions of the adaptive subgoal-selection rule and the long-edge penalty, and a hyperparameter sweep (τ, T) provides useful practical guidance and shows the method is not brittle within a reasonable range.

The paper reports wall-clock overhead (graph construction, per-episode search, per-step selection), which supports the practicality claims, and favorably compares against more heavily engineered baselines (GAS, CompDiffuser) that require additional training, showing competitive or superior results in several settings despite using strictly less privileged machinery.
Presentation is generally clear, with helpful visualizations (distance fields, guide paths, motivating failure-mode figure) that aid intuition.
weaknesses: Gains are highly base-learner- and environment-dependent: on several tasks (e.g., antmaze-giant-navigate-v0, humanoidmaze-giant-navigate-v0 with GCIQL/QRL, and most visual-humanoidmaze tasks) both the base learner and TTGS remain near 0%, indicating the method cannot rescue fundamentally poor value functions/policies, which somewhat tempers the generality claims made in the abstract and conclusion.

Despite claims that TTGS requires 'no additional supervision' and is 'simple to adopt', Table 4 shows per-dataset, per-agent tuning of τ and T (and sometimes M), which implies some validation-based hyperparameter search is needed in practice, partially undercutting the simplicity narrative.

The comparison to GAS and CompDiffuser in Table 3 is explicitly acknowledged as an unequal comparison (different settings, missing entries denoted '/'), which limits how much can be concluded from claims of 'surpassing substantially more complex methods.'

No ablation isolates whether the value-derived distance meaningfully outperforms a much simpler baseline such as chaining consecutive states from the same trajectory or generic nearest-neighbor stitching without any value-function signal; this would help substantiate that the value-based distance itself (rather than just having any subgoal decomposition) is doing the work.

Evaluation is restricted to locomotion/maze navigation domains in OGBench; no manipulation or non-navigation tasks are tested, so it is unclear how well the geometric assumptions underlying the graph search (e.g., short local hops being reliable) transfer to non-spatial or higher-dimensional goal-reaching problems.

The distance-to-steps closed-form mapping (Section 3.1) is derived under two specific reward conventions (sparse terminal, per-step penalty); it is unclear how robust or easy to derive/calibrate this mapping is for other value parameterizations or reward shaping schemes commonly used in practice.

Storage/memory requirements for retaining the full offline dataset (or a large M=4000 subset) at test time for graph construction are not discussed as a limitation, despite claims of being 'lightweight'; this could be a practical concern in large-scale or resource-constrained deployments.

Standard deviations in several tables are very large relative to the means (e.g., antmaze-large-explore-v0: 26.6 ± 34.0), raising questions about the robustness/significance of some of the reported improvements, though the paper does not report formal significance tests beyond an informal 95%-of-best bolding convention.

strengths: The method is simple, training-free, and easy to retrofit onto any pretrained value-based GCRL policy, with minimal computational overhead reported (graph build ~45-100s, per-episode search ~0.8s, per-step overhead ~1ms).

The paper identifies a clear and intuitive failure mode (policies work well at short horizons but fail at long horizons) and backs it with a dedicated motivating figure (Fig. 2) showing success rate degradation with horizon length.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided for the two key design choices (adaptive subgoal selection vs. greedy next-waypoint, and the edge-length penalty), as well as a hyperparameter sensitivity sweep over τ and T.
The framework is shown to work with two different kinds of distance signals (value-derived and a simple domain-specific body-position L2 distance), suggesting some flexibility.

Large absolute gains are reported in several near-zero-baseline settings (e.g., pointmaze-giant-stitch, humanoidmaze-giant-stitch), which is a meaningful practical demonstration that one-shot execution is a real bottleneck.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core recipe (sample dataset states as graph nodes, compute edge costs from a learned/value-derived or geometric distance, run shortest-path search, execute subgoals with a frozen policy) closely follows a well-established line of prior work (Eysenbach et al. 2019 'Search on the Replay Buffer', Savinov et al. 2018, Zhang et al. 2021 latent landmarks, Emmons et al. 2020 sparse graphical memory, and especially the concurrent GAS paper). The main technical additions here are an edge-penalty reweighting scheme and an adaptive farthest-reachable-subgoal heuristic, which are incremental engineering choices rather than a new principle.

The headline claim that TTGS 'sometimes surpasses substantially more complex methods' is not well supported by the full results table (Table 3): GAS, which requires additional training, outperforms HIQL+TTGS by a wide margin on most antmaze and humanoidmaze-giant-navigate tasks (e.g., antmaze-large-explore: GAS 91.0 vs. TTGS 26.6; humanoidmaze-giant-navigate: GAS 14.0 vs. HIQL+TTGS 85.3 only in one case but GAS wins on most antmaze variants). The main text selectively emphasizes the favorable pointmaze/humanoidmaze-stitch cases while underplaying the many settings where GAS or even the base learner without TTGS is competitive or superior, which overstates the method's generality.

Results are inconsistent across base learners: QRL+TTGS sometimes underperforms QRL alone (e.g., antmaze-giant-navigate-v0: 10.8 vs. 11.8; antmaze-large-explore-v0: 0.0 vs 0.0), and GCIQL+TTGS remains near-floor on several antmaze/humanoidmaze tasks (e.g., 0.2-5.4%), undermining the claim of 'consistent' improvement. Many visual-domain tasks (e.g., visual-humanoidmaze-medium-*) show both base and TTGS near 0%, indicating the approach provides no benefit when the underlying value function/policy is poor, which is a substantial limitation of the 'any value-based learner' framing.

High variance in several reported results (e.g., 26.6 ± 34.0, 32.2 ± 17.3) raises concerns about the robustness and statistical reliability of the reported gains; no significance tests are reported despite large standard deviations relative to means.

Despite claims of being 'simple to adopt' and not requiring training, Table 4 shows that τ and T are hand-tuned per dataset and per base agent, effectively requiring a small grid search for each new environment/agent combination, which weakens the practical simplicity argument.

The theoretical justification for the value-derived distance is weak: the paper acknowledges the predicted distances may violate the triangle inequality, be asymmetric, and be optimistic/biased, but does not provide any analysis of how these violations affect planning correctness or error accumulation, relying entirely on empirical tuning (e.g., the ad hoc superlinear penalty function p(x) = x·1000^(x/τ)) to patch over these issues.

The domain-specific L2 (body-position) distance experiment, which performs comparably to or even better than the value-derived distance in several environments (Table 1), somewhat undercuts the central narrative that the contribution is specifically about 'unlocking' geometric structure already encoded in a value function, since a trivial non-learned Euclidean heuristic achieves similar gains.

Comparisons are restricted to the hardest/largest maze variants in the main text; it is unclear how TTGS performs on medium/small or less stitching-heavy tasks, raising a possible selection bias in which settings are highlighted.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practically appealing: a training-free, inference-time graph-search wrapper that reuses an already-trained goal-conditioned value function as an edge-cost signal, requiring no changes to the base learner's training pipeline.

Figure 2 provides a clear and convincing diagnostic for the motivation: success rate of multiple base learners (GCIQL, HIQL, QRL) degrades sharply as the number of steps to the goal increases, directly motivating the subgoal-decomposition approach.

The method derives closed-form value-to-distance mappings for common reward conventions (sparse terminal and per-step penalty), making the approach concretely applicable to several widely-used base learners (HIQL, GCIQL, QRL) without hand-crafted metrics.

Experiments span many OGBench locomotion environments (pointmaze, antmaze, humanoidmaze, visual variants) and multiple base learners, with results averaged over 8 seeds and 50 rollouts per task, which is a reasonably thorough empirical protocol.

Useful ablations isolate the contributions of adaptive subgoal selection and the edge-length penalty, and a sensitivity analysis over the threshold hyperparameters (τ, T) is provided, along with a domain-specific distance variant that demonstrates the generality of the graph-search framework beyond value-derived distances.
Reported computational overhead (graph construction ~45-100s, per-episode planning ~0.8s, per-step ~1ms) is modest and supports the practicality claim.
The limitations section is reasonably forthright about dependence on base-learner quality and distance-estimator accuracy.
weaknesses: Per-environment, per-agent hyperparameters (τ, T in Table 4) were apparently selected per dataset/agent combination, but the paper does not describe a principled, held-out tuning protocol; since these are tuned presumably by observing success rate on the same evaluation tasks, there is a risk of overfitting hyperparameters to the test metric, which undermines the 'no additional supervision' framing and complicates reproducibility for new environments.

The comparison against GAS and CompDiffuser in Table 3 and the abstract/intro claim of 'surpassing substantially more complex methods' is selectively emphasized: GAS actually outperforms TTGS by a wide margin on many tasks (e.g., antmaze-giant-navigate-v0, most visual-antmaze tasks, antmaze-large-explore-v0), and the comparison itself is explicitly acknowledged by the authors to be an unfair, differently-scoped setting (GAS uses additional training and a learned low-level controller), making the 'surpasses' framing somewhat overstated.

The value-derived distance predictor is explicitly non-metric (may violate triangle inequality/symmetry) and the shortest-path search assumes meaningful edge costs; the justification for why Dijkstra search over such a non-metric graph remains sound is empirical rather than theoretical, so the paper offers no formal guarantee or failure analysis for cases where the value function is substantially miscalibrated.

Several results exhibit very high variance (e.g., antmaze-large-explore-v0: 26.6 ± 34.0, i.e., std larger than the mean), raising questions about the robustness and statistical reliability of the reported gains in these settings.

No ablation isolates the contribution of the graph/Dijkstra search itself versus a simpler baseline (e.g., nearest-neighbor subgoal chaining without explicit shortest-path search, or random waypoint selection), which would help clarify how much of the gain comes from graph search specifically versus merely breaking a long horizon into short hops.

Domain-specific distance (agent body position) requires access to body-position information beyond the raw observation in several cases, which is in slight tension with the abstract's claim of using 'any state-space distance' with 'no privileged information.'

Evaluation is restricted to locomotion/maze navigation tasks in OGBench; the benchmark also includes manipulation domains that are not tested, leaving the generality of the approach to other GCRL settings (e.g., manipulation, robotic control with contact dynamics) unverified.

When base learners are fundamentally unreliable (e.g., GCIQL on several antmaze/humanoidmaze tasks remains near 0% even with TTGS), the method provides little benefit, indicating the approach's gains are contingent on a baseline quality threshold that is not deeply characterized.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and empirically validated: existing GCRL value functions already encode enough local geometric structure to support graph-based test-time planning, without any additional training. This is a nice re-framing / negative result against the implicit assumption in prior work that value functions are too noisy for planning.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five base learners (HIQL, QRL, GCIQL, SAW, OTA) and a large number of OGBench tasks (locomotion, manipulation, pixel-based variants), with substantial and consistent gains on long-horizon stitching tasks (e.g., near-zero to >90% success in several settings).

Thorough ablation studies (soft vs hard penalty, adaptive subgoal selection vs naive next-waypoint, clustering vs random sampling, replanning vs one-shot planning, sensitivity to τ and T, scaling in M) that meaningfully support the design choices.

The proposed soft-penalty edge weighting mechanism is a sensible and well-justified solution to the graph-disconnection problem caused by hard thresholding, and its benefit is clearly demonstrated (Table 10, Appendix H).
Negligible computational overhead is convincingly demonstrated (Appendix I), supporting practicality claims.

The hop-ratio diagnostic (ρ) is a useful and low-cost tool for practitioners to predict a priori whether TTGS will help, and its validity is reasonably supported by the manipulation vs. locomotion comparison.

Honest discussion of limitations and failure conditions (dataset coverage, base-policy local reliability), including the humanoidmaze counterexample where low ρ does not guarantee gains, strengthens the credibility of the claims.

Comparisons against GAS and CompDiffuser, despite operating in a more constrained (training-free) setting, and against a simple L2-kNN landmark baseline, help contextualize the contribution's significance.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior graph-based planning approaches for GCRL (SoRB, SGM, VMG, GAS, etc.); the core mechanism (graph over dataset states + Dijkstra + subgoal execution) is a fairly standard landmark-planning recipe, and the main new ingredient is the soft-penalty edge weighting and adaptive subgoal selection heuristic, which, while effective, are relatively simple engineering contributions.

The value-to-distance mapping f(V) relies on specific closed-form reward conventions (sparse terminal / per-step penalty) and requires per-base-learner derivations (Appendix B); it is unclear how robust/general this mapping is to base learners with different or more complex reward/value parameterizations beyond the five tested.

Manipulation results show TTGS provides essentially no benefit (0-2pp gains), and the paper's explanation (lack of intermediate states) is plausible but the diagnostic and framework does not offer a path to improving performance in these settings beyond future work suggestions, limiting the generality of the contribution's claimed significance.

Hyperparameter selection (τ, T) is described as a manual, qualitative process based on visual inspection of shortest paths, which raises reproducibility concerns and may not scale well to new domains without significant human-in-the-loop tuning, despite claims of simplicity.

The comparison to GAS/CompDiffuser is somewhat apples-to-oranges since those methods operate under different assumptions (training additional components); while the paper acknowledges this, the 'competitive with' framing in the abstract/intro could be seen as slightly overstating the comparison given TTGS underperforms GAS on several tasks (e.g., antmaze-giant-stitch, antmaze-large-explore in Table 4).

The theoretical justification for why local value estimates are trustworthy while long-range ones are not is largely empirical/intuitive (Figure 2c, Appendix D) rather than grounded in a formal error-accumulation analysis, which would strengthen the core claim.
Only OGBench is used for evaluation; generalization to other GCRL benchmarks or real-world robotic settings is not demonstrated, which somewhat limits claims of broad significance.

strengths: The empirical evaluation is extensive: five base learners (HIQL, QRL, GCIQL, SAW, OTA), many OGBench locomotion variants (medium/large/giant, navigate/stitch/explore, state and visual), and comparisons against GAS and CompDiffuser, with 8-seed averages and consistent protocol.

The soft-penalty edge weighting is a well-motivated and empirically validated design choice: Table 10 and Appendix H convincingly show that hard-thresholding disconnects the graph on stitching tasks (disconnect ratios up to 0.99) while the soft penalty preserves connectivity and dramatically improves success rate.

Thorough ablation and diagnostic suite: adaptive subgoal selection vs. naive next-waypoint, clustering vs. random vertex sampling, replanning vs. one-shot planning, triangle-inequality violation analysis, scaling sweep over graph size M, and runtime breakdown — all of which support reproducibility and give a reasonably complete picture of what drives the method's performance.

The largest-hop-ratio diagnostic (Section 4.3) is a cheap, useful, rollout-free tool that cleanly separates regimes where TTGS helps (locomotion) from where it does not (manipulation), adding practical value beyond the core algorithm.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly documents when TTGS fails to help (manipulation tasks with poor dataset coverage), acknowledges dataset-access requirements at test time, and frames failure modes clearly (base-policy local unreliability vs. planner infeasibility).

Gains on the hardest stitching tasks are substantial (e.g., HIQL from 0% to ~80-90% on several giant mazes), and the method is compute-cheap (<1s planning, ~1.5ms per-step overhead), making it an attractive practical tool if the claims hold up.
weaknesses: The central conceptual novelty is thinner than advertised: landmark/graph search over a learned distance function with a connectivity-preserving edge rule is methodologically close to prior graph-based planners (SoRB, SGM, Savinov et al. 2018); the paper's framing that prior work "assumes value functions are too unreliable" is somewhat overstated given SoRB already attempted graph search over value-derived distances, with the main delta here being the soft- vs. hard-threshold penalty and an adaptive subgoal rule, which are comparatively incremental contributions.

The L2-kNN ablation (Appendix E) undercuts the paper's headline claim that the value function's "latent geometric structure" is being specifically unlocked: a purely domain-agnostic Euclidean-position graph search achieves performance within a few points of the value-derived variant when k is well-tuned, suggesting much of the gain comes from the graph-search/subgoal-decomposition mechanism itself rather than from value-function geometry specifically.

Despite being framed as "lightweight" and requiring "no additional supervision," TTGS in practice needs per-dataset, per-base-learner tuning of (τ, T) (Table 14 shows dozens of distinct hyperparameter settings), and the tuning procedure described (Appendix L) is informal/qualitative (visual inspection of path fragmentation), which weakens reproducibility and the "minimal overhead" framing — this is a nontrivial practical cost that is understated in the main text.

The method's benefit is concentrated almost entirely in maze/locomotion domains with dense state coverage; on manipulation tasks, where arguably practitioners most need better long-horizon planning, gains are negligible (0-2pp), and the paper does not propose or test concrete remedies beyond speculation (synthetic state generation, improved value learning) in the limitations section.

Comparisons to GAS/CompDiffuser, while interesting, are not fully apples-to-apples: TTGS is tuned per-task while the "fixed-hyperparameter" comparison (Table 5) only tests one direction (GAS's antmaze-tuned hyperparameters transferred elsewhere) without an analogous test of TTGS hyperparameters transferred without any task-specific adjustment from the start, leaving open how much of TTGS's apparent robustness advantage is due to its own implicit tuning.

The theoretical grounding remains largely empirical/heuristic (no formal guarantee on path feasibility or error bounds under compounding value errors); the triangle-inequality analysis in Appendix D, while a nice sanity check, is correlational and does not establish when/why local consistency should hold across arbitrary GCRL value functions and architectures.

strengths: Strong empirical validation: TTGS is evaluated across five diverse base learners (HIQL, QRL, GCIQL, SAW, OTA) and a wide range of OGBench tasks (pointmaze, antmaze, humanoidmaze, visual variants, manipulation), with consistent and often dramatic gains on long-horizon stitching tasks (e.g., near-zero to >90% success).

The core idea is simple, practical, and training-free, making it easy to adopt on top of already-trained policies without retraining or online interaction, which is a meaningful practical contribution given the common deployment scenario described.

Thorough ablations and diagnostics: the paper carefully isolates the contribution of the soft-penalty mechanism vs. hard thresholding (Appendix H), adaptive subgoal selection vs. naive next-waypoint selection (Fig 4a), vertex sampling strategy (clustering vs. random, Appendix G), and the L2-kNN baseline (Appendix E), each with clear quantitative support.

The proposed hop-ratio diagnostic (Section 4.3) is a useful, cheap, rollout-free heuristic for predicting whether TTGS will help, and is validated to separate locomotion (low ratio, large gains) from manipulation (high ratio, minimal gains).

Honest and detailed limitations discussion, including runtime breakdown (Appendix I), failure mode analysis, dataset-access requirements, and explicit acknowledgment of when the method does not help (manipulation tasks) without claiming otherwise.

Good reproducibility support: extensive appendices provide value-to-distance derivations per base learner (Appendix B), hyperparameter tables for every dataset/learner combination (Appendix L), and scaling/runtime sweeps (Appendix I.1).
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the soft-penalty mechanism is largely heuristic (hand-chosen exponential penalty form p(x) = x·1000^{x/τ}); while ablations show it helps, there is no principled derivation of why this specific functional form is optimal or how it should scale with the degree of value-function miscalibration across domains.

Comparisons to GAS and CompDiffuser (Table 4, Appendix A) are not run under identical evaluation protocols—numbers are taken from original papers or their official repos, with different training pipelines and possibly different goal/seed distributions—so claims of being 'competitive with' these methods should be interpreted cautiously despite the authors' transparency about this limitation.

Hyperparameter selection (τ, T) relies on a manual, qualitative inspection procedure (Appendix L) tried on 1-2 seeds per setting rather than a systematic validation protocol, which could inflate reported performance via implicit tuning on test environments and makes it less clear how a practitioner would select these values a priori on a genuinely new task without the benchmark's known structure.

Gains on manipulation tasks are negligible (0-2 pp), and while the paper attributes this to lack of dataset coverage and provides supporting visualizations, this somewhat narrows the scope of real-world applicability to settings resembling locomotion/navigation with locally dense data; the method's value proposition is weaker outside this regime.

The method requires retaining access to (a sample of) the offline dataset at test time, which, while discussed as a minor limitation, is a meaningful deployment constraint not shared by purely parametric policies, and the compute/memory overhead of maintaining and querying the graph at scale (quadratic in M for graph construction) could become significant for much larger or higher-dimensional datasets than tested.
